extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of poetics (writers of tragedy/epic)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing tragic (and epic) poetry and drama: how to plan a fable, order episodes and names, preserve probability/visibility on stage, and use gesture and passion to move an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw the plan of the subject first
rubrics_metrics.description: YATE ought first to draw the Plan of the Subject, to write it, as exactly as possible, to thus reviewing carefully all its parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the plan in lofty prose, review it often, act as the first spectator and judge what effects it will have; examine it with the stage in mind and at every apparent action ask why it is done, why an actor enters or exits, so to find and correct faults before the piece is finished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy is imitation of a visible action (unity & visibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Imitation is an Action, which passes into Representation, not recitation, and consequently is the imitation of a visible Action; Tragedy is the Representation of one Action only, from which it necessarily follows, that that Action ought to be publick, and visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The action should be apparent to the audience on stage; avoid staging actions that supposedly occur in distant places without making them visible or probable to spectators (criticizes devices that pretend the audience saw what they did not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not persuade the audience they saw what they did not
rubrics_metrics.description: None must pretend to persuade the Audience, that they see what they don't see, and that they don't see what they really behold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never rely on the audience accepting implausible stage fictions; maintain probability/verisimilitude so spectators are not 'cheated' into believing impossible stage events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place of the scene ought to be public
rubrics_metrics.description: The place of the Scene ought to be publick, since the action ought to be so, and that place being publick, not one Actor ought to appear there without a necessity for't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer public settings for the scene because tragic action should be public and visible; avoid private apartments as default scene-locations unless strong reasons make it probable that figures of state would appear there publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrances/exits must have clear necessity, especially at first scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Not one Actor ought to appear there without a necessity for't, and that necessity ought to be greater, and more prevalent in the first Scene, than in all the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The audience should be able to understand why actors enter or leave; the opening scene requires especially strong justification for who is present and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience must know what actors do during intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: It ceases to be a Tragedy, when [actors] have nothing to do [during intervals]; the Audience should know what the Actors are doing during the Intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave gaps where actors appear idle offstage; continuity of the action requires credible offstage activity or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order the fable in general before episodes or names
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a Poet write on a Subject already known, or invents a new one, 'tis necessary that he orders his Fable in general, before he thinks of making his Episodes, and to Circumstantiate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First create a universal, general statement of the fable (the subject) without names or particular circumstances; only afterwards add names and episodes so as not to make the fable particular too early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give names to actors, then compose episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Fable is made, the Names must be given to the Actors, and the Episodes made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning names after the general fable lets the poet adapt episodes drawn from historical or character-traits associated with those names; names influence which episodes will be appropriate and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be proper (appropriate & necessary to the fable and names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Due regard must be had, that the Episodes be proper... they ought to be necessary, and natural parts of the action itself; taken from the very foundation of the Fable in relation to the names of the Persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes should arise from the subject and characters (e.g., Orestes' madness and deliverance by expiations are proper to his story); if names were different, appropriate episodes would change—episodes must not be generic add-ons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes short in dramatic poetry, extended in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: The Episodes are short in a Dramatick Poem, but Epopœia is extended and amplified by those that belong to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because tragedy is representation and confined (e.g., to one day), episodes must be brief; epic being recitative and without fixed time allows long, amplified episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix truth and fiction skillfully (use historical truth to render fable credible)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fiction is the Fable the Truth are the Episodes, drawn from the real actions of those from whom the names are borrowed. 'And mixes Truth and Fiction skillfully, That nothing in the whole may disagree.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When borrowing names from history or myth, utilize real actions (truths) as episodes to lend credibility and make the invented fable more probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate gestures, voice, and air of the characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet must also as much as possible imitate the Gestures, and Actions of these, whom he makes to speak... imitate the Gestures, Voice, and Air of him whom he makes to speak, for by this means, he will find all that is agreeable to the Character which he represents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization should extend into physical comportment and vocal manner; using such imitation supplies details appropriate to the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with passion—be moved to move the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: For 'tis certain, that take two Men, who are of an Equal Genius, he that is in a Passion shall always be the most persuasive... he who is truly moved, shall move those which hear him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To produce convincing speech and action, the poet/actor must feel the passions he depicts; method and frequent imitation of passions (heat before exactness) help produce persuasive writing/acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet needs an excellent genius or fury (natural talent or inspired fervor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Therefore a Poet to succeed well, ought to have an excellent Genus, or to be Furious, for the enraged are easily susceptible of all Figures and Characters, and the excellent Genius are fruitful, and Inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success in poetry arises either from refined natural talent or a kind of inspired madness that supplies invention and emotional force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose great and serious subjects (not trifles)
rubrics_metrics.description: That which makes the Subject of a Tragedy ought not to be a Trifle, but a great and a serious Action, and there is no Prince but would go out of his Palace on such an account as this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The stakes of a tragic subject must be weighty enough to justify public action and the scale appropriate to tragedy; avoid trivial incidents as core subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot and unravelling: distinct structural parts
rubrics_metrics.description: I call the Plot all that part of the Tragedy, from the beginning to that place where the affairs change their face. I call the unravelling all that is from that change, to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the action up to the peripeteia (plot) from the sequence after the turning-point (unravelling); both should be well-constructed and the poet should aim to succeed in both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy admits several sorts; skill to succeed in the different kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: We have said, that Tragedy has four parts... The first is the implex Tragedy... The second is the Pathetic... The third is the Moral... The fourth... that is transacted in Hell... We should endeavour to succeed in all these four sorts, or at least in the greatest part of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the different modes/forms of tragedy (implex, pathetic, moral, chthonic/other) and aim to master the particular strengths appropriate to the kind you write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic material should dilate and increase the principal action (not merely add-ons)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must take notice, that the Episodes are not added to the principal Action, but only dilate and encrease that principal Action; that is to say, that every part of the Fable, being told singly, is the matter and grounds of an Episode... thereby rendered proper and necessary to the Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use episodes to expand and illuminate the central action—make them integral so they feel necessary rather than detachable adventure-stories.
